10a.html:
Given: cuprite (\mathrm{Cu_2O}) ore with 15.42% Cu by mass; atomic masses Cu = 63.55, O = 16.00.

Find: the percentage of gangue in the ore.

Assumptions: all the copper is present as cuprite, and everything that is not cuprite is gangue. Basis: 100 g of ore.

Step 1, copper content of cuprite.

\begin{aligned} M_{\mathrm{Cu_2O}} &= 2(63.55) + 16.00 = 143.10\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}} \\ \text{mass fraction of Cu in } \mathrm{Cu_2O} &= \frac{2(63.55)}{143.10} = \frac{127.10}{143.10} = 0.8882 \end{aligned}

Step 2, cuprite in the ore. The 15.42 g of Cu in 100 g of ore is carried by

m_{\mathrm{Cu_2O}} = \frac{15.42\ \mathrm{g}}{0.8882} = 15.42 \times \frac{143.10}{127.10} = 17.36\ \mathrm{g}

Step 3, gangue.

m_{\text{gangue}} = 100 - 17.36 = 82.64\ \mathrm{g\ per\ 100\ g\ of\ ore}

Check: the cuprite holds 17.36 - 15.42 = 1.94 g of O, that is 0.121 mol O against 15.42/63.55 = 0.243 mol Cu, a Cu to O ratio of 2 to 1 as in \mathrm{Cu_2O}.

Answer: the ore contains about 17.4% cuprite and 82.6% gangue (82.64% by mass).
pts: States the assumptions (all Cu present as \mathrm{Cu_2O}, the rest is gangue) and a basis of 100 g of ore
Molar mass of cuprite M_{\mathrm{Cu_2O}} = 2(63.55) + 16.00 = 143.1\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}
Mass fraction of Cu in cuprite 127.1/143.1 = 0.888 (88.8% Cu)
Cuprite in the ore 15.42/0.888 = 17.36\%
Final answer: gangue = 100 - 17.36 = 82.6\% by mass
Checks the result, for example by the 2 to 1 mole ratio of Cu to O

10a.watch:
• The commonest slip is 100 - 15.42 = 84.58\%: the oxygen bound in the cuprite is part of the value mineral, not gangue.
  • The same calculation with 10.38% Cu gives 11.69% cuprite and 88.31% gangue. Using Cu = 63.5 instead of 63.55 changes the answer by less than 0.01%.
  • If the ore also held another copper mineral (for example malachite), the cuprite content could not be found from the Cu assay alone; the assumption that all Cu is in \mathrm{Cu_2O} must be stated.

10b.html:
Artificial bed (ragging): a layer of coarse particles placed on the jig screen, which

  • are coarser than the screen apertures (and than the feed), so they stay on the screen;
  • have a density between those of the value mineral and the gangue, for example haematite or magnetite for a galena-quartz feed.

On pulsion the ragging opens up; on suction the fine dense particles work down through its gaps and the screen into the hutch. Light particles cannot penetrate it and leave over the end as tailings. The size, density and depth of the ragging set the cut.

When it is used: when the feed is fine (finer than the screen apertures) and the dense mineral is recovered through the screen as hutch product, or when the feed holds too little heavy mineral to form a natural bed. (With coarse feed the feed itself forms the bed.)
pts: Defines ragging as a layer of coarse particles placed on the jig screen, coarser than the screen apertures
States that its density lies between those of the mineral and the gangue
Explains the action: fine dense particles pass down through the ragging and screen into the hutch while light particles are rejected as tailings
When used: fine feed whose dense product is taken through the screen as hutch product, or feed with too little heavy mineral to form its own bed

11a.html:
The flowing film. When a thin film of water flows down a flat, slightly inclined surface, the water next to the surface is held back by friction with the water adsorbed on it, so its velocity is zero at the deck and rises toward the free surface. For a laminar film of depth h on a slope \alpha the profile is parabolic:

u(y) = \frac{\rho g \sin\alpha}{\mu}\left(hy - \frac{y^2}{2}\right)

where y is the height above the deck.

Action on particles. Each particle is pushed by the water at its own height.

  1. Size: a small particle is immersed in the slow layer next to the deck, while a large one reaches into the faster layers, so small particles move more slowly than large ones.
  2. Density: at the same size, a dense particle presses harder on the deck (more weight and friction against the same drag), so dense particles move more slowly than light ones.

So fine dense particles move slowest and coarse light ones fastest, and a lateral movement develops between them. Fine light and coarse dense particles can travel at similar speeds, so the feed should be closely sized.

Use on the shaking table. The wash water flows across the deck as such a film. The fast, coarse light particles are swept across the riffles to the tailings side; the slow, fine dense particles stay in the riffles and are moved along the deck by the shaking to the concentrate end.
pts: Water velocity is zero at the deck (friction) and increases toward the surface, with the profile shown or stated
Small particles lie in the slow layer and move more slowly than large particles
Dense particles move more slowly than light particles of the same size
Result: fine dense slowest, coarse light fastest, so coarse light is separated from fine dense (and close sizing is needed)
Links to the shaking table: cross-flowing wash water carries coarse light particles to the tailings side while dense particles stay in the riffles and move to the concentrate end
Neat sketch: deck, film, velocity profile, flow direction, particles of different size and density labelled

Mineral: a naturally occurring, solid, crystalline, mostly inorganic compound whose composition varies only within narrow limits and whose physical properties are well defined, for example galena (PbS) and chalcopyrite (\mathrm{CuFeS_2}).

Ore: a natural aggregate of value minerals and gangue from which a metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently, for example bauxite for aluminium.

12.html:
Conductivity and the type of bonding

Electrical conduction needs charge carriers that are free to move, and the type of bonding decides how free the bonding electrons are.

  1. Metallic bonding: the valence electrons are delocalised over the whole crystal (an electron gas), so conductivity is very high (resistivity about 10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\mathrm{m}), as in native copper.
  2. Ionic bonding: electrons are held tightly by the ions, so there are no free electrons. Current can flow only by slow migration of ions, which is negligible at room temperature, so halite, calcite and fluorite are insulators (they conduct when molten or dissolved).
  3. Covalent bonding: electrons are localised in bonds between neighbouring atoms. With a large band gap (quartz about 9 eV) the solid is an insulator, above about 10^{10}\ \Omega\,\mathrm{m}; with a small gap it is a semiconductor whose conductivity rises with temperature.
  4. Mixed covalent-metallic bonding in many sulphides and some oxides (galena, band gap about 0.4 eV; pyrite, chalcopyrite, pyrrhotite, magnetite) gives semiconductors and fairly good conductors, roughly 10^{-5} to 10^{2}\ \Omega\,\mathrm{m}.

So conductivity follows directly from bonding, and mineral conductivities span more than 20 orders of magnitude.

Why ore structure controls resistivity

An ore is an aggregate: conducting grains (sulphides, magnetite) in an insulating silicate or carbonate gangue. Current follows only continuous paths.

  • If the sulphide is disseminated as isolated grains, every path must cross insulating gangue between grains, so the ore's resistivity stays high, close to that of the host rock, even with a large sulphide content.
  • If the same or a smaller amount forms connected veinlets, stringers or a massive body, the current runs through the sulphide network and resistivity is low.
  • The rest of the conduction is electrolytic, through pore water, and depends on porosity, pore connectivity, water content and salinity, which are also features of structure. Banded ores conduct better along the bands than across them.

Hence resistivity depends on how the conductors are connected (texture, porosity, orientation) more than on their volume fraction. A massive sulphide body shows up clearly in resistivity prospecting, while a disseminated ore may not.
pts: Metallic bonding: delocalised free electrons give high conductivity (resistivity about 10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\mathrm{m}), as in native metals
Ionic bonding: electrons bound to ions, conduction only by ion migration, so insulators at room temperature
Covalent bonding: localised electrons; large band gap gives an insulator (quartz), small gap a semiconductor
Sulphides and some oxides with partly metallic bonding are semiconductors or good conductors (galena, pyrite, magnetite), with a wide range of values
Concludes that conductivity follows the freedom of the bonding electrons, over many orders of magnitude
An ore is conducting grains in insulating gangue, and current needs a continuous path
Disseminated isolated grains give high resistivity even at high content; connected veinlets or massive ore give low resistivity even at low content
Pore water (porosity, connectivity, salinity) or the orientation of bands also controls resistivity
Gives a consequence, for example massive versus disseminated sulphide in resistivity prospecting, or locked particles reporting as middlings in electrostatic separation

  • "Structure" here means the ore texture (how the grains are arranged and connected), not the crystal structure of one mineral.

1a.html:
Smelting and matte smelting

Smelting (reduction smelting) heats an ore, usually an oxide, with a flux and a reducing agent (coke) so that the oxide is reduced and the charge melts into liquid metal and an immiscible slag, with gases leaving:

\text{mineral} + \text{gangue} + \text{flux} + \text{reducing agent} \rightarrow \text{metal} + \text{slag} + \text{gas}, \qquad \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{M} + \mathrm{CO}

Matte smelting fuses a sulphide concentrate (usually partly roasted) with a flux, without a reducing agent, to give a matte, a molten mixture of sulphides (\mathrm{Cu_2S} and FeS), under an immiscible slag; some sulphur leaves as \mathrm{SO_2}.

BasisSmeltingMatte smelting
Chargeoxide ore, flux, cokesulphide concentrate or calcine, siliceous flux
Chemistryreduction by C and COmainly melting; Fe partly oxidised and slagged
Atmospherereducingneutral to mildly oxidising
Productcrude metal (iron, lead)matte, an intermediate that must be converted
GasCO, \mathrm{CO_2}\mathrm{SO_2}

Extraction of copper by matte smelting

The process works because copper has a greater affinity for sulphur, and iron a greater affinity for oxygen: iron is oxidised and slagged, and copper stays as \mathrm{Cu_2S}.

  1. Concentration. Chalcopyrite (\mathrm{CuFeS_2}) ore with less than 2% Cu is upgraded by froth flotation to a concentrate of about 11 to 35% Cu.
  2. Partial roasting. Part of the FeS is oxidised; the reaction is not completed, so that no higher iron oxides form:
2\,\mathrm{CuFeS_2} + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + 2\,\mathrm{FeS} + \mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad 2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}
  1. Matte smelting. The calcine is melted with quartz at 1200 to 1300 °C (reverberatory or flash furnace). Any copper oxide is turned back to sulphide, and FeO is slagged:
\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{FeS} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{FeO}, \qquad \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}

The denser matte collects below the slag; the slag is tapped off and discarded.

  1. Converting. Air is blown through the molten matte. Slag blow: FeS is oxidised and slagged, and the slag is poured off, leaving white metal (\mathrm{Cu_2S}):
2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}

Copper blow:

2\,\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}, \qquad 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\,\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}

The product is blister copper, about 99% Cu.

  1. Refining. Fire refining blows air to remove the dissolved sulphur ([\mathrm{S}] + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{SO_2}), then removes the dissolved oxygen with hydrocarbons (poling), for example \mathrm{CH_4} + 3\,[\mathrm{O}] = \mathrm{CO} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}; S falls from about 0.02 to 0.002% and O from 0.5 to 0.05%. The anodes are electrorefined to cathode copper of 99.99% Cu.
pts: Smelting: ore, flux and a reducing agent (coke) heated to give liquid metal, slag and gas, with a reduction such as \mathrm{MO} + \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{M} + \mathrm{CO}
Matte smelting: sulphide charge fused with flux, no reducing agent, gives a matte (molten \mathrm{Cu_2S} + FeS) and an immiscible slag
At least two contrasts: metal against an intermediate that needs converting, reducing against neutral or oxidising conditions, oxide against sulphide feed, CO against \mathrm{SO_2}
Principle: Cu has the greater affinity for S and Fe for O, so Fe goes to slag and Cu to matte (or gives the sequence concentration, roasting, smelting, converting, refining)
Concentration of chalcopyrite (below 2% Cu) by froth flotation to about 11 to 35% Cu

Partial roasting with balanced reactions (2\mathrm{CuFeS_2} + \mathrm{O_2} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + 2\mathrm{FeS} + \mathrm{SO_2}; 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2}), not taken to completion

Matte smelting with silica at 1200 to 1300 °C: \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}, and \mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{FeS} = \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{FeO} or "very little reaction, mainly melting"
Matte and slag immiscible; the denser matte settles below and the slag is removed
Converting, slag blow: 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and slagging with \mathrm{SiO_2}; slag poured off
Converting, copper blow: 2\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}, giving blister copper of about 99% Cu
Refining: fire refining (S oxidised by air, O removed by hydrocarbons or poling) and electrorefining to about 99.99% Cu

  • Do not write that carbon reduces the matte: matte smelting needs no reducing agent, and copper is made from \mathrm{Cu_2S} by the reaction of \mathrm{Cu_2O} with \mathrm{Cu_2S} in the converter.
  • The roast is stopped short because \mathrm{Fe_3O_4} and \mathrm{Fe_2O_3} melt high and are hard to slag; magnetite makes the slag viscous and traps matte.
  • The slide says matte has twice the specific gravity of slag; typical values are about 5 and 3.5, so a ratio near 1.5. The point that the matte sinks is what earns the mark.

1b.html:
Zone refining purifies a metal that is already fairly pure. A narrow molten zone is moved slowly along a solid bar; impurities that lower the melting point collect in the liquid, travel with the zone to the far end, and that end is cut off. It gives ultra-pure Si, Ge, Ga and Al.

Technique. The partly purified bar or rod is held horizontally or vertically in an inert container under inert gas or vacuum. A ring heater melts a short zone at one end and moves slowly along the bar: the zone melts impure charge at its front, and crystallised solid freezes at its back.

Principle from the phase diagram. When the impurity lowers the melting point, the liquidus and the solidus both fall from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus more steeply. At every temperature the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium with it:

k = \frac{C_S}{C_L} < 1

A melt of composition X (C_0) starts to freeze at L_1 and deposits solid S_1 with only kC_0; the rejected impurity enriches the liquid towards L_2.

Effect of the moving zone. The solid freezing at the back of the zone is purer than the zone liquid, so the rejected impurity stays in the zone and is carried forward. After one pass (Pfann):

\frac{C_S}{C_0} = 1 - (1 - k)\,e^{-kx/l}

where l is the zone length: the first solid holds kC_0, and the last zone length freezes impure and is cropped.

Multiple passes. Passes are repeated in the same direction; the more passes, the purer the starting end. For k = 0.3 the start holds 0.3C_0 after one pass and about 0.01C_0 after five. Several heaters along the bar give several passes at once.

Conditions. The separation is good when k is far from 1, and the zone must move slowly so that freezing stays near equilibrium. Impurities with k > 1 (they raise the melting point) move the other way, to the starting end.
pts: Defines zone refining: a narrow molten zone moved along a solid bar sweeps the impurities into the liquid and to one end, which is cut off
Technique: partly purified bar or rod in an inert container or atmosphere; a heater melts a zone at one end and moves it slowly along the length
Phase diagram: temperature against impurity concentration, liquidus and solidus falling from T_m of the pure metal, three fields labelled, tie lines S_1L_1 and S_2L_2
States from the diagram that the solid holds less impurity than the liquid in equilibrium, k = C_S/C_L < 1 (S_1 purer than L_1)
The purer solid freezes at the back of the zone, the rejected impurity stays in the zone and is carried forward; the last part is impure and cropped
Multiple passes in the same direction raise the purity at the starting end
First solid holds kC_0, or quotes the Pfann single-pass equation
A condition or use: k far from 1, slow zone travel, impurities with k > 1 move to the starting end, or products such as Si, Ge, Ga

• Axes: temperature (vertical) against impurity (solute) concentration (horizontal).
  • Liquidus and solidus both falling from T_m of the pure metal, the solidus below and steeper.
  • Fields labelled Liquid, Solid + Liquid, Solid.

1b.watch:
• The phase diagram carries the marks for "principles": label the axes, both lines and the tie line, and say which composition is the solid.
  • Do not say the impurity "evaporates" or is "removed" in the zone: it is only redistributed along the bar, and the impure end must be cut off.
  • Fast zone travel lets the rejected impurity build up ahead of the freezing front, so the effective k moves towards 1 and each pass removes much less impurity.
  • Extra depth: silicon is refined by the floating-zone method (no container) because molten Si reacts with crucible materials and picks up oxygen and other contamination; after many passes the profile reaches a limiting (ultimate) distribution, set by k and the zone length.

2a.html:
Common types of leaching reagents

  1. Water: dissolves soluble salts such as \mathrm{CuSO_4} and \mathrm{ZnSO_4}; some poor copper sulphide ores slowly turn into water-soluble sulphate in air. Plain water is rarely used alone.
  2. Acids: mineral acids, above all \mathrm{H_2SO_4}, are the most common reagents; their strong action often makes fine grinding unnecessary, and acid consumed in leaching is regenerated during electrolysis.
  3. Bases: hot, concentrated NaOH under pressure for bauxite; \mathrm{NH_4OH} for native copper, copper ores, NiS and \mathrm{Cu_2S}.
  4. Aqueous salt solutions: NaCN for gold (with oxygen); \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} for scheelite (\mathrm{CaWO_4}).

Oxidising or reducing secondary reagents (\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}, \mathrm{O_2}, \mathrm{SO_2}) are often added to help dissolution.

Criteria for selecting an effective reagent

  1. Selectivity: it should dissolve the value mineral and leave the gangue; selectivity depends on the reagent concentration, temperature and contact time.
  2. Rate: it should be soluble enough to make a strong solution that leaches fast and keeps the handled volume small.
  3. Cost and regeneration: it should be cheap and preferably recoverable for recycling.
  4. Corrosion and safety: it should not corrode the plant (chloride solutions are severe) and should be non-toxic, to cut capital, maintenance and hazard.
  5. Character of the material: the chemical and physical nature of the ore decides which reagent can attack it.

Selectivity and cost are the most important factors.
pts: Water, with soluble sulphates as the example, and the note that plain water is rarely used alone

2b.html:
The leaching reagent R reacts at the mineral surface to give a soluble metal species M and other products P. Two situations can arise (see the sketches).

(a) The mineral dissolves completely. All the products are soluble, so the surface simply recedes and no solid layer forms, for example \mathrm{ZnO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2O}. Across the liquid boundary film the reagent falls from [R]_B in the bulk to [R]_S at the surface, while M and P are highest at the surface and fall to [M]_B and [P]_B. Kinetic steps:

  1. diffusion of R from the bulk of the solution to the mineral-solution interface;
  2. reaction of R with the mineral surface to form the soluble metal species;
  3. diffusion of M (and P) away from the interface into the bulk.

(b) The mineral decomposes and dissolves in parts. An insoluble product, or the undissolved part of the ore, stays behind as a porous residue around the unreacted mineral; leaching goes on only if this layer is porous. Example: \mathrm{CaWO_4(s) + CO_3^{2-} \rightarrow CaCO_3(s) + WO_4^{2-}}. I is the mineral-residue interface and II the residue-solution interface. This is the more general case. Kinetic steps:

  1. diffusion of R from the bulk to the residue-solution interface II;
  2. diffusion of R through the porous residue to I;
  3. reaction of R with the mineral at I to form soluble M;
  4. outward diffusion of M and P through the porous layer;
  5. diffusion of M and P from II into the bulk.

Case (a) lacks steps 2 and 4. The slowest step, or a combination, controls the rate.

Accelerating the leaching. The right method depends on the rate-controlling step, so find it first:

  • Stirring test: if the rate rises with stirring speed, film diffusion (step 1 or 5) controls; stirring or agitation thins the boundary layer and steepens the gradients. Beyond a certain speed the rate levels off and more stirring is wasted.
  • Chemical reaction control (step 3): agitation has no effect. Raise the temperature: the activation energy is about 10 to 25 kcal/mol (42 to 105 kJ/mol), so the rate is very sensitive to it. Raise the reagent concentration (its effect follows the reaction order).
  • Temperature speeds up all the steps, but diffusion only weakly (5 kcal/mol, 21 kJ/mol, or less), so diffusion control becomes more likely at high temperature.
  • Pore diffusion (steps 2 and 4) and surface area: grind finer; 10 mm to 0.1 mm gives 100 times the area per unit mass and a shorter path through the residue. Roasting, micro-cracks and other pretreatments make the solid porous and more reactive.
  • Oxidant supply: where \mathrm{O_2} is a reactant (gold in cyanide), a higher oxygen pressure in an autoclave raises its dissolved concentration and the rate; bacteria speed up sulphide leaching by reoxidising \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} to \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}.
pts: Sketch (a): mineral, solution and boundary film, with [R] rising from [R]_S to [R]_B and [M], [P] falling from the surface to the bulk
Sketch (b): mineral, porous residue with interfaces I and II, and the [R], [M], [P] profiles across residue and film
Explains situation (a): complete dissolution with soluble products and no solid layer, with an example
Explains situation (b): partial decomposition leaving a porous residue (leaching goes on only if it is porous), with an example
Three steps for (a): diffusion of R in, surface reaction, diffusion of M and P out
Five steps for (b): film diffusion of R, pore diffusion of R, reaction at I, pore diffusion of M and P, film diffusion of M and P
Stirring speeds up leaching when film diffusion (step 1 or 5) controls, up to a limiting speed
When the chemical reaction (step 3) controls, agitation has no effect; raise temperature or reagent concentration
Temperature speeds up all steps; reaction is far more sensitive (about 10 to 25 kcal/mol) than diffusion (5 kcal/mol or less)
Finer grinding (more area, shorter pore path) or a pretreatment such as roasting that makes the solid porous
Higher oxidant supply (oxygen pressure, autoclave) or bacterial action

3a.html:
Purpose

Leaching is rarely selective, so the pregnant liquor carries impurity ions that interfere with later steps or contaminate the product. Solvent extraction (liquid-liquid extraction) removes the desired metal selectively and leaves the impurities behind; with selective precipitation and ion exchange it is one of the purification methods.

Principle

The metal is separated from the aqueous liquor by preferential dissolution in an organic phase that is almost immiscible with water. The organic phase is an extractant (higher alkyl amines \mathrm{R_3N}, diethyl ether; for copper a hydroxyoxime) usually dissolved in a diluent such as kerosene. The split of a metal between the phases is the distribution coefficient

D = \frac{[\mathrm{M}]_{\text{org}}}{[\mathrm{M}]_{\text{aq}}}

A good extractant gives a high D for the wanted metal and a low D for the impurities. With D = 10 and equal volumes, one contact extracts 10/11 \approx 91\ \%, so several stages are used.

Stages

  1. Dissolution: the ore is leached in an acid or alkaline aqueous medium.
  2. Extraction and decontamination: the organic is agitated with the liquor to a fine dispersion (large contact area); metal ions enter the organic phase, impurity ions stay in the aqueous raffinate.
  3. Partition: the phases settle; the lighter organic floats on the aqueous and the layers are separated.
  4. Stripping: the loaded organic is contacted with a fresh, impurity-free aqueous solution. This (a) recovers the metal as a pure, concentrated solution and (b) regenerates the extractant for recycle. Several loaded metals can be stripped selectively by adjusting the pH, or the metal can be precipitated straight from the organic.

Example: uranium (amine extractant)

\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{2R_3N + 2H^+ + SO_4^{2-} \rightleftharpoons (R_3NH)_2SO_4}\\ &\mathrm{2(R_3NH)_2SO_4 + [UO_2(SO_4)_3]^{4-} \rightleftharpoons (R_3NH)_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 2SO_4^{2-}}\\ &\mathrm{(R_3NH)_4UO_2(SO_4)_3 + 5Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow 4R_3N + Na_4UO_2(CO_3)_3 + 3Na_2SO_4 + 2CO_2 + 2H_2O}\\ &\mathrm{2Na_4UO_2(CO_3)_3 + 6NaOH \rightarrow Na_2U_2O_7 + 6Na_2CO_3 + 3H_2O} \end{aligned}

The amine first takes up acid, then exchanges sulphate for the uranyl sulphate anion; the impurity cations stay in the raffinate. Sodium carbonate strips the uranium and frees the amine, and NaOH precipitates sodium diuranate.

Example: copper (SX-EW)

\mathrm{2RH_{(org)} + Cu^{2+}_{(aq)} \rightleftharpoons R_2Cu_{(org)} + 2H^+_{(aq)}}

Extraction runs at low acidity; strong sulphuric acid (spent electrolyte) reverses it, giving a pure, concentrated \mathrm{CuSO_4} electrolyte for electrowinning, while most of the iron stays in the raffinate.

Practice

Mixer-settlers in counter-current stages carry out extraction and stripping, with the organic recycled in a closed loop.

3b.html:
Percolation (vat or sand) leaching passes the leach solution through a stationary bed of crushed low-grade ore held in large vats or tanks.

Preparation. The ore is crushed to about 5 to 20 mm, large enough for the solution to flow freely through the voids. Fines and clay are removed, because they block the bed.

Procedure.

  1. The ore is loaded into the vats, which are then filled with leaching solution.
  2. After the solution has been in contact with the ore for a set time, it is drawn off and fresh solution is added.
  3. Several stages are needed, run on the counter-current principle in a series of vats, the solution from one vat cycling to the next. The freshest (strongest) solution enters the vat whose ore has been leached longest, and the newest ore meets the weak (spent) solution that has already passed the other vats.
  4. So the particles that are hardest to dissolve meet the strongest solution, while the fresh ore is still readily attacked by the weak one. The solution leaving the fresh-ore vat is the most concentrated pregnant solution, sent to metal recovery.
  5. At each step one vat is being loaded with fresh ore and one is being washed and emptied; then the feed point moves on by one vat (step 1 to step 2 in the sketch).
  6. When its leaching cycle is complete, the ore is washed with water one or more times and the leached ore (tailings) is removed.

Performance. With 10 or more leach cycles, 80 to 90% of the metal values are recovered; in the reading's copper example, 90.4% from 1.6% Cu ore with dilute \mathrm{H_2SO_4}. It is a batch process, since vats are idle while charged and emptied, yet it is the most efficient method found for leaching large tonnages of low-grade ore.
pts: Sketch: a series of vats with ore beds and the solution passing from the bottom of one vat to the top of the next

Ore crushed to about 5 to 20 mm, with fines and clay removed so the bed stays permeable
Vats filled with solution, contact for a set time, solution drawn off and fresh solution added
Counter-current principle: strongest solution to the longest-leached ore, weak (spent) solution to the fresh ore, with the reason
The cycle moves on: one vat loading and one unloading at each step
Washing with water and removal of tailings at the end; 10 or more cycles recover 80 to 90%
Batch process, but the most efficient method for large tonnages of low-grade ore (for example copper ore with dilute acid)

4a.html:
An electrolyte for metal extraction or refining should:

  1. High ionic conductivity, so the IR drop and energy are low.
  2. High solubility of the metal salt, giving a high metal-ion concentration (cryolite dissolves \mathrm{Al_2O_3}).
  3. Stability: only the wanted metal is discharged; other constituents have higher decomposition voltages and do not volatilise or hydrolyse.
  4. No attack on the deposit, electrodes or cell lining; a dense, adherent deposit.
  5. Cheap, easily purified and regenerated. A fused-salt bath also needs a low melting point and a density different from the metal.
pts: High electrical (ionic) conductivity, to keep the voltage and energy low
High solubility of the metal compound, giving an adequate metal-ion concentration
Chemical and electrochemical stability: no constituent other than the metal is discharged, no volatilisation or hydrolysis
No chemical attack on the deposit, electrodes or cell materials (a sound deposit results)
Cheap, easily purified and regenerated, or (fused salt) low melting point and a density different from the metal

4b.html:
An impurity behaves according to its electrode potential relative to the metal being treated and to whether it forms soluble ions. Copper electrorefining is the standard example.

In electrorefining (impurities in the anode)

  1. Nobler than the metal (Au, Ag, Pt metals in Cu; E^\circ well above +0.34 V): they do not dissolve and fall as anode slime and are recovered. A little chloride precipitates any dissolved Ag as AgCl.
  2. Less noble (Ni -0.25, Fe -0.44, Zn -0.76 V): they dissolve with the copper and accumulate in the electrolyte but do not deposit (far more negative potentials). As they build up they replace \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} and raise the resistance, so part of the electrolyte is bled (Ni recovered as \mathrm{NiSO_4}).
  3. Close to the metal (As, Sb, Bi, standard potentials about +0.2 to +0.3 V): they partly dissolve and partly go to slime. They may co-deposit or form fine "floating slime" that is occluded in the cathode, so they are the most harmful. They are controlled by bleeding, liberator cells and keeping enough As to precipitate Sb and Bi.
  4. Insoluble compounds: selenides and tellurides (\mathrm{Cu_2Se}, \mathrm{Ag_2Se}, \mathrm{Cu_2Te}) go to slime; Pb forms insoluble \mathrm{PbSO_4}; Sn forms an insoluble basic salt. \mathrm{Cu_2O} dissolves chemically, \mathrm{Cu_2O + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + Cu + H_2O}, enriching the electrolyte in copper.

In electrowinning (impurities in the electrolyte)

  1. Nobler ions (Cu, Cd, Co in zinc electrolyte) co-deposit, so the solution is purified first (zinc-dust cementation).
  2. Ions that lower the hydrogen overvoltage (Co, Ni, Sb, Ge) start hydrogen evolution and re-dissolve the zinc deposit; the current efficiency can collapse.
  3. Redox ions (\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}, \mathrm{MnO_4^-/Mn^{2+}}) are reduced at the cathode and re-oxidised at the anode, wasting current. Chloride can evolve \mathrm{Cl_2} and corrode lead anodes.

Conclusion: noble impurities report to slime, base ones to the electrolyte, and those near the metal's potential, or those that lower hydrogen overvoltage, threaten cathode purity and efficiency.
pts: Classifies impurities by electrode potential relative to the metal being refined or won
Nobler impurities (Au, Ag, Pt metals) do not dissolve and report to the anode slime (Ag fixed as AgCl by chloride)
Less noble impurities (Ni, Fe, Zn) dissolve and accumulate in the electrolyte without depositing; they lower the \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} content, so the electrolyte is bled and purified
Impurities close in potential (As, Sb, Bi) partly dissolve, may co-deposit or form floating slime; controlled by bleeding, liberator cells
Insoluble compounds: selenides, tellurides, \mathrm{PbSO_4}, tin salts go to slime; \mathrm{Cu_2O} dissolves chemically and enriches the electrolyte
Electrowinning: nobler ions co-deposit, so the leach liquor is purified first (e.g. cementation)
Electrowinning: impurities that lower hydrogen overvoltage (Co, Ni, Sb, Ge) or redox ions (\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}) lower the current efficiency
Concludes which group threatens cathode purity and which threatens efficiency

4c.html:
Aluminium (E^\circ = -1.66 V) cannot be deposited from water, so it is won by fused-salt electrolysis of alumina dissolved in cryolite (Hall-Heroult process, 1886).

Raw material. Bauxite is purified by the Bayer process (NaOH digestion, red mud rejected, \mathrm{Al(OH)_3} precipitated and calcined) to pure \mathrm{Al_2O_3}.

Electrolyte. Molten cryolite, \mathrm{Na_3AlF_6}, with about 2-6 % \mathrm{Al_2O_3}, excess \mathrm{AlF_3} and about 5 % \mathrm{CaF_2}, at about 950-970 ^\circC. Cryolite dissolves alumina (m.p. 2050 ^\circC) at a much lower temperature, conducts well, and its density (about 2.1 g/cm^3) is below that of liquid Al (about 2.3 g/cm^3), so the metal collects under the bath, protected from air.

Cell. A steel shell lined with insulation and carbon blocks (cathode, with steel collector bars); a pool of molten Al is the working cathode surface. Carbon anodes (prebaked or Soderberg) dip into the bath about 4-5 cm above the metal. A frozen crust covered with alumina insulates the top and frozen bath protects the side walls.

Reactions.

\text{cathode: } \mathrm{Al^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Al(l)} \qquad \text{anode: } \mathrm{2O^{2-} + C \rightarrow CO_2 + 4e^-}
\text{overall: } \mathrm{2Al_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Al + 3CO_2}

The anode burns away (theory 0.33, practice about 0.4-0.45 kg C per kg Al), which lowers the reversible voltage from about 2.2 V to about 1.2 V.

Operation. About 4-4.5 V per cell, 150-500 kA, current efficiency 90-96 %, energy about 12.5-15 kWh per kg Al. Alumina is fed through the crust by point feeders. If it falls below about 2 %, the anode effect occurs: the voltage jumps to 20-50 V and \mathrm{CF_4} forms. Aluminium (about 99.7 %) is siphoned off daily and cast; off-gas fluorides are caught on alumina in dry scrubbers and returned.

Role of cryolite: dissolves alumina at about 950-970 ^\circC (alumina melts at 2050 ^\circC), conducts, and is lighter than liquid Al so the metal sinks
Bath composition: about 2-6 % \mathrm{Al_2O_3} with \mathrm{AlF_3} and \mathrm{CaF_2} additions
Electrode reactions and the balanced overall reaction \mathrm{2Al_2O_3 + 3C \rightarrow 4Al + 3CO_2}, with anode consumption
Operating data: about 4-4.5 V, current efficiency about 90-96 %, energy about 12.5-15 kWh/kg Al
Alumina feeding through the crust and the anode effect at low alumina
Tapping of 99.7 % Al and fluoride capture on alumina in the off-gas scrubber

5a.html:
An undersize particle does not pass at once:

  • Screen matrix. Only part of the screen is open, so a particle may hit the wire. The chance per presentation is P = [(D_A - d)/(D_A + D_W)]^2: about 6% for d = 0.5D_A with D_W = D_A, so some 36 presentations give a 90% chance. Particles must be presented many times.
  • Blinding. Particles just larger than the aperture wedge in the openings.

Moving the screen solves both:

  • Vertical movement lifts particles out of the blocking positions and loosens the bed so fines reach the deck.
  • Horizontal movement makes the particles, when they fall back, land at different positions on the screen, and carries the oversize along.

Vertical motion alone drops a particle on the same aperture; sliding alone leaves blinding particles wedged. Hence a vibrating screen is far more efficient than a static bar screen.
pts: A particle meets the screen matrix as well as apertures, so it must be presented many times to pass (probability of passage less than 1)
Near-mesh particles blind the apertures
Vertical movement lifts particles out of the blocking positions (unblinding) and lets fines work through the bed
Horizontal movement presents the falling particles at different positions on the screen and moves the oversize along
Conclusion: a vibrating screen gives both movements and is far more efficient than a static bar screen

5b.html:
Basic chance (sphere, perpendicular approach). A sphere of diameter d passes a square aperture of side D_A only if its centre lands inside the inner square of side D_A - d; the cell, with wire D_W, has side D_A + D_W:

P = \left(\frac{D_A - d}{D_A + D_W}\right)^2

With D_W = D_A: P = 20\% at d = 0.1D_A but 1\% at d = 0.8D_A. After n presentations the chance is 1 - (1-P)^n.

Angle of approach.

  • A particle approaching perpendicular to the screen sees the full aperture: highest chance of passage.
  • An oblique approach (at \theta to the normal) sees a projected opening of only about D_A\cos\theta. A 0.8D_A particle cannot pass beyond about 37^\circ (\cos\theta = 0.8).
  • So steep or fast decks pass near-mesh particles poorly; vibration that makes particles drop nearly vertically helps.

Particle orientation.

  • A non-spherical particle presents a small cross-section in some orientations and a large one in others.
  • Plate-like mica lies flat and "rides" over the apertures, so it screens extremely badly; on edge it would pass.
  • Elongated grains pass only end-on; tumbling on a moving screen tries more orientations.

A particle passes most readily when it is small relative to the aperture, near-spherical and arrives perpendicular to the screen.

6a.html:
Industrial screening is rarely used below about 200 μm because a fine screen cannot handle a high throughput.

1. Capacity falls in proportion to the aperture (example). Take two screens of 1 ft² and 80% open area: aperture a with 100 openings, and 0.1a with 10,000 openings. If both feeds screen equally easily, n particles pass each opening per minute. The particle just passing has volume a^3 on the coarse screen and 0.001a^3 on the fine one:

\begin{aligned} \text{coarse: } & 100\,n\,a^3 \\ \text{fine: } & 10{,}000\,n\,(0.001a^3) = 10\,n\,a^3 \end{aligned}

The fine screen passes ten times less material; the permissible feed rate is roughly proportional to the aperture.

2. Open area falls. With wires of the same diameter, the open area [D_A/(D_A + D_W)]^2 for 0.1 mm wire is 91% at 2 mm aperture but 44% at 0.2 mm, so the chance of passage per attempt falls.

3. Weak surface. Very thin wires restore the open area but make the screen fragile.

4. Blinding and moisture. Near-mesh fines blind the apertures; damp fines agglomerate.

Example in practice. A ball mill grinding to about 75 μm is closed with a hydrocyclone or rake classifier, not a screen.
pts: States the reason: at fine apertures a screen cannot handle high throughputs, so capacity per unit area is very low
Works the two-screen example: 100 openings of a against 10,000 of 0.1a; volumes 100na^3 against 10na^3, so the fine screen passes ten times less
Open area decreases with finer aperture for the same wire size, lowering the probability of passage
Thin wires needed for open area make the screen fragile, so strength becomes limiting
Blinding by near-mesh particles and agglomeration of damp fines
Practical example: fine separations (closing a grinding circuit) use classifiers such as hydrocyclones instead of screens

Free settlingHindered settling
MeaningSinking in a fluid volume that is large compared with the total particle volumeSinking in a crowded pulp
SolidsBelow about 15% solids by weight (well-dispersed pulp)Higher solids content
Particle interactionCrowding negligible; each particle falls on its ownCrowding and collisions slow every particle
Effective mediumThe carrier liquid (water)The pulp acts as a heavy liquid of pulp density
Settling rateHighest, set by the particle and the liquidLower
Controlling factorSize has the larger effectDensity has the larger effect; size matters less
ClassifiersHorizontal-current (sedimentation) classifiersVertical-current classifiers

Why density matters more when hindered. The driving force depends on the density difference between particle and medium. For galena (7.5) and quartz (2.7):

\frac{7.5 - 1.0}{2.7 - 1.0} = 3.8 \ \text{in water}, \qquad \frac{7.5 - 1.5}{2.7 - 1.5} = 5.0 \ \text{in a pulp of density 1.5}

The lighter particle is slowed far more, so hindered settling sharpens separation by density.
pts: Free settling: particles settle in a large volume of fluid, crowding negligible, below about 15% solids by weight
Hindered settling: at higher solids, crowding reduces the falling rate and the pulp behaves as a heavy liquid of pulp density

7a.html:
Thickening is the cheapest dewatering method but leaves 40-50 % water; filtration is dearer and leaves about 10 %; drying, the dearest, leaves none.

Thickening and filtration remove water as a liquid, mechanically, by gravity settling (cost mainly capital) and by a pressure difference across a cloth, with no phase change.

Drying must convert the water to vapour: heat raises it to the boiling point and supplies the large latent heat of evaporation (2257 kJ/kg at 100 C), about 2.57 MJ per kg of water from 25 C, all from fuel. Heat is also lost to the solids and exhaust gas, and the gas raises dust.

A 10 % filter cake still holds 111 kg of water per tonne of dry solids (about 0.29 GJ). So water is removed mechanically first, and drying only takes the last part.
pts: States the comparison: thickening cheapest (40-50 % water left), filtration dearer (about 10 %), drying dearest (zero)
Thickening and filtration remove liquid water mechanically, with little energy (thickening cost mainly capital)
Drying must evaporate the water, needing sensible heat and the large latent heat of evaporation (about 2260 kJ/kg), from fuel
Extra losses (exhaust gas, heating the solids, dust) or the conclusion that mechanical dewatering is done first and drying only removes the last water

7b.html:
Frothers are heteropolar, surface-active organic reagents added in small amounts (50-300 g/t), for example pine oil, cresylic acid or eucalyptus oil.

Action. The polar group (for example -\mathrm{OH}) is hydrated by water, while the non-polar hydrocarbon chain is pushed into the air. The molecules therefore concentrate at the air-water interface, polar end in the water and chain in the air, and lower the surface tension. They must be partly soluble in water, or they will not spread evenly.

Role in the separation.

  1. Stable bubbles: after the collector has made the mineral hydrophobic, the loaded bubbles must reach the surface without bursting; a burst bubble releases its particles back into the pulp.
  2. Stable froth: at the top of the cell the frother keeps a froth that holds the mineral until it is skimmed into the launder.
  3. Not too stable: an over-stable froth is hard to handle, so the dose is kept small.
  4. Finer bubbles: lower surface tension gives smaller, more numerous bubbles and more surface for particles to attach to.

Ideally the frother acts only in the liquid and does not change the mineral's floatability.
pts: Defines frothers as heteropolar surface-active organic reagents used in small amounts, with an example (pine oil, cresylic acid)
Explains that they adsorb at the air-water interface (polar group in water, chain in air) and lower the surface tension
Role: stabilise the bubbles so they carry the mineral to the surface and form a froth that can be skimmed; otherwise bubbles burst and drop the load
Notes that the froth must not be too stable, because it then cannot be handled
Notes that ideally the frother has practically no effect on the mineral's floatability (or that it must be partly water-soluble, or gives finer bubbles)

8a.html:
Reduction ratio is the ratio of the maximum size of the particles in the feed to the maximum size of the particles in the product. It is a convenient figure for comparing the performance of different crushing machines.

For a crusher it is calculated from the machine itself as gape over set:

\text{reduction ratio} = \frac{\text{gape (opening at the mouth)}}{\text{set (opening at the throat)}}

For example, a 66 x 84 in jaw crusher (66 in gape) with a 6 in set has a calculated ratio of 66/6 = 11. A single stage usually achieves about 5:1, so size reduction is done in several stages.

Why the actual ratio is usually smaller:

  1. The feed is smaller than the gape. The calculation assumes the largest feed piece is as big as the gape. In practice the largest pieces are usually smaller than the gape, and the average piece is considerably smaller.
  2. Product larger than the set. Rock is discharged mostly while the swing jaw is receding, so pieces larger than the minimum throat opening, some almost as large as the maximum opening, escape.
  3. Wear of the jaw faces enlarges the set unless it is adjusted.
  4. Flat slabs can slip through a jaw crusher unbroken.
pts: Defines reduction ratio as the maximum feed size over the maximum product size, used to compare crushers
Calculated ratio for a crusher is gape over set, with the set as the opening at the throat
A worked example (such as 66/6 = 11) or the note that a stage gives about 5:1
Reason: the largest feed pieces are smaller than the gape and the average piece much smaller
Reason: discharge mostly while the jaw recedes, so pieces larger than the minimum throat opening escape
Reason: wear of the jaw faces enlarges the set
Reason: flat slabs pass through unbroken

8b.html:
Fast compression (impact) is stress applied at a very high rate, as when a hammer strikes a particle or a falling ball lands on the charge.

Mechanism.

  1. Rock contains pre-existing cracks. Under slow loading the stress rises only until the largest crack grows; the stress is relieved and the particle splits into a few large pieces.
  2. Under impact the stress rises faster than any crack can relieve it, far above the level needed for the largest crack.
  3. So the existing cracks are extended, small ones included, and new cracks are formed at the same time.
  4. The many cracks join and the particle shatters.

Result: fragments much smaller than the original, with a broad size distribution and many fines.

Where it occurs: hammer mills, stamp mills, and the impact zone (toe) of a ball mill.
pts: States that fast compression is stress applied rapidly (impact), for example a hammer blow or a falling ball
Explains that existing cracks are extended and new cracks are formed, so fracture occurs at many places
Gives the reason: the stress rises faster than cracks can relieve it, far above that needed to propagate the largest crack
Result: fragments much smaller than the original, broad distribution with many fines, contrasted with the few large pieces of slow compression
Names a machine or zone where it acts (hammer mill, stamp mill, impact zone of a ball mill)

• "Describe the mechanism" needs the crack story: extension of old cracks plus formation of new ones. A bare "the particle breaks into small pieces" earns little.
  • Strain rate is one of the factors in Table 2.1 of the book reading that set the strength of rock; the same rock breaks finer under impact than under slow loading.

9a.html:
Given: feed spheres of radius r = 0.75 in; product spheres of radius 0.25 in; angle of nip 2\alpha = 32.4^\circ.

Find: the diameter D = 2R of the rolls.

Assumptions: the product size equals the roll gap, so the gap is d = 2(0.25) = 0.50 in; the angle of nip is the angle between the two tangents at the points of contact, 2\alpha, so \alpha = 16.2^\circ.

Step 1, geometry. A sphere just nipped touches both rolls. The line from a roll centre to the sphere centre has length R + r; its horizontal projection is R + d/2, and it makes the angle \alpha with the line of roll centres:

\cos\alpha = \frac{R + d/2}{R + r}

Step 2, solve for R.

\begin{aligned} \cos 16.2^\circ &= 0.9603 \\ R + 0.25 &= 0.9603\,(R + 0.75) \\ R\,(1 - 0.9603) &= 0.9603 \times 0.75 - 0.25 = 0.4702 \\ R &= \frac{0.4702}{0.0397} = 11.84\ \mathrm{in} \end{aligned}

Step 3, diameter.

D = 2R = 23.7\ \mathrm{in} = 23.7 \times 0.0254 = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}

Check: \tan 16.2^\circ = 0.29, a normal coefficient of friction between steel rolls and rock, so a 32.4^\circ nip is the usual limit.

Answer: the rolls should be about 23.7 in (0.60 m) in diameter, roughly 24 in.
pts: Takes the roll gap as the product size, d = 0.50 in (product radius 0.25 in)
Writes the nip geometry \cos\alpha = (R + d/2)/(R + r) with r = 0.75 in
States the convention and uses the half angle \alpha = 32.4/2 = 16.2^\circ, \cos\alpha = 0.9603 (or states that the angle of nip is taken as \alpha itself and uses \cos 32.4^\circ = 0.8443)
Solves the linear equation correctly: R = 0.4702/0.0397
Roll radius R = 11.8 in
Final answer D \approx 23.7 in (about 0.60 m), with units; with the stated reading \alpha = 32.4^\circ, D \approx 4.9 in (0.125 m)

9a.watch:
• Read the angle of nip as the full angle between the tangents, 2\alpha: its usual limit is about 32^\circ (\tan 16.2^\circ = 0.29), which is why the paper prints 32.4^\circ. Some texts call \alpha itself the angle of nip; that reading gives D = 4.9 in, rolls that would need \mu = 0.63 to nip 1.5 in lumps. State which angle you use.
  • Work in radii throughout: the feed and product are given as radii, and the half gap d/2 equals the product radius, 0.25 in.
  • A roll diameter about 16 times the feed diameter (23.7/1.5) is typical of smooth rolls: they nip only small particles, so they give small reduction ratios (here 3:1).

9b.html:
A toothed roll crusher carries teeth, corrugations or breaker bars on its rolls (two rolls, or one roll against a stationary breaker plate). Smooth rolls break by compression alone. Advantages of toothed rolls:

  1. Not limited by nip. Smooth rolls grip a lump only if the angle of nip is below about 32^\circ, so they take only small lumps. Teeth bite into the lump, so toothed rolls reduce much larger particles.
  2. Several breaking actions: compression, impact and shear, so they are much more versatile.
  3. Tear weak, ductile feed. The teeth tear the particles apart, which suits weak, ductile or soft materials (coal, shale) that smooth rolls would only flatten.
  4. One roll can do the work against a breaker plate.

Limitation: they cannot handle very hard solids; smooth rolls are used there, and where few fines and no oversize are wanted.
pts: Not limited by the nip angle, so it can take much larger feed particles than smooth rolls of the same size
Breaks by compression, impact and shear (smooth rolls by compression only), so it is more versatile
Teeth tear the particles apart, so it suits weak, ductile or soft materials
Describes the construction: teeth, corrugations or breaker bars; two rolls or one roll against a breaker plate
States the limitation: not for very hard solids (smooth rolls give few fines and no oversize)
